title: Advice to look thick for tall/wide lifters (compound movements & technique)
summary: Part 2 of NH's advice for tall and wide lifters, this time practical. He recommends sumo deadlifts and low-bar squats as the main lifts, puts most posterior-chain and leg volume on safer variations, and tells tall lifters to widen their grips and stances, superset isolation with compounds, and stop comparing their strength or size to average-height lifters.
claims: Most fitness YouTubers are average height, roughly 5'7 to 5'10, so they do not understand the problems tall lifters face, and their cookie-cutter advice will not work for you
NH is 6 feet, at the cutoff for tall, and says every inch above that adds more difficulty
Tall lifters need a longer technical adaptation stage to find a squat stance that does not wreck the lower back; it can take weeks for a 5'4 lifter but much longer for you
Do not be afraid of stepping back from a lift that feels sketchy: preventing an injury might take three weeks, curing one might take three months
Lifting is a game of patience for tall lifters: it takes longer, but once you reach the required level you will be massive
Squats and deadlifts move the most weight and drive the most hypertrophy, but tall lifters have to approach them differently
High-bar squats and conventional deadlifts are very hard for tall lifters because their longer torsos force more forward lean and make lumbar and thoracic rounding more common
If you are tall and can high-bar and pull conventional without pain or form breakdown, keep doing them
Tall lifters should try the sumo deadlift: it lets them keep a neutral spine and still trains the hamstrings and glutes hard while loading the lower back less
Longer distance between head and hips means more torque on a tall lifter's lower back, so anything that spares the lower back is gold
Use the sumo as your main strength pull from the floor, but do not use sumo variations as accessories the way powerlifters do; take most posterior-chain volume and tonnage from other lifts
Stiff-leg and Romanian deadlifts suit tall lifters: with a long torso you can bring it parallel to the floor and control lumbar rounding by stopping where you need to
Tall lifters who want to keep heavy conventionals should do rack or block pulls from whatever height works; as long as the bar starts below the kneecap you still get hamstring and glute work
If you have wide shoulders, take a wider grip on the deadlift, and do not hesitate to widen your stance
Hyperextensions and reverse glute-ham raises are great for tall lifters, and you can move some volume from the sumo to them because they are safer
The squat is the biggest problem for tall lifters: a long torso plus long legs means more range of motion and more forward lean, a recipe for lower back injury
A tall lifter covers more range of motion than a short one even on a block pull, so do not be ashamed of using the range that suits your build
On low bar, tall lifters should not go ass-to-grass; the hips tuck under past parallel and the lumbar spine rounds (butt wink), which adds needless stress, so a power squat to about parallel is fine
Low bar is the best squat for tall lifters because you start already bent forward and the bar sits lower, so the lower back can stay rigid like a bridge instead of flexing during the rep
The lower back can hold any angle safely as long as it stays stationary; what is dangerous is flexion that happens during the movement, for example at the bottom of a high-bar squat
If shoulder mobility makes low bar hard, use a false grip with the thumb not wrapped; the forward lean keeps the bar secure on the back
Use low bar as the main squat, then add high-bar pause squats to parallel, front squats or safety-bar squats instead of getting all the volume from the main lift
Hypertrophy is a game of years, so a technique that lets you squat for five years beats one that only lasts one year, in tonnage and in everything else
Tall or wide lifters should widen their bench grip rather than putting their pinkies on the rings; it can be easier on the shoulders and stronger

Long-armed benchers already move the bar further, so adjust the touch point and work on the arch to reduce range and shoulder flexion; the best range of motion is the one you can repeat day after day without injury
The overhead press tends to give tall lifters the fewest problems, and tall lifters often do well on pull-ups despite the extra range
Tall lifters need diffuse tonnage across every body part, so they should lean on compounds that carry over to small muscles (bench for triceps, chin-ups for biceps) and then add isolation
Superset isolation movements with compound variations whenever possible; it may tax the cardiovascular system at first but it is the best way to fit both in
Long arms take a long time to look impressive, but once they do they look very impressive
Tall lifters have greater absolute strength because of their bigger frame, so they should not compare strength with shorter lifters; strength does not correlate with muscle size
A tall lifter might squat 500 lb before his legs look impressive, while some lifters have massive legs with a 315 squat

Enhanced giants have stepped on stage at 6 feet and above, but there are almost no examples of very tall naturals who got big, because it takes so long, injuries are more likely and the advice they get hurts them
Size comes from safely accumulating tonnage within relevant intensity windows; strength helps by raising tonnage per session, but maxing out all the time will not make you big
